body:
Wendy’s WEN-Q on Thursday rejected a US$1.4-billion take-private offer from activist investor Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and its partners, and adopted a “poison pill” plan to resist pressure from one of its largest shareholders.

The food chain’s limited-duration shareholder rights plan aims to stop investors from amassing more than 15 per cent of the company, and is intended to prevent any shareholder from gaining control without paying all shareholders an appropriate premium, Wendy’s said in a regulatory filing.

Trian and related parties own a 16.3-per-cent stake in Wendy’s, according to a regulatory filing.

If triggered, the rights plan would let existing shareholders purchase stock at a discount, reducing the value of the would-be acquirer’s stake.

Wendy’s said the measure is designed to give its board and a committee of independent directors time to evaluate takeover proposals and pursue alternatives that maximize shareholder value.

Peltz was partnering with restaurant operator Flynn Group and investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners on the proposed acquisition, looking to revive the U.S. fast-food chain’s struggling sales away from the glare of public-market investors.

“The proposal substantially undervalues the company,” the independent board committee created to evaluate the offer said.

Trian, which considered taking Wendy’s private in 2022 and backed away in 2023, has campaigned to change strategy and board composition at various companies including Walt Disney, Kraft Heinz and Procter & Gamble.

The activist investor declined to comment.

In recent years, buyout firms have tried to purchase other publicly traded restaurants, including Papa John’s, which has fended off offers from Irth Capital and Apollo Global over the last year.

Wendy’s shares see-sawed in premarket trading after it also reported weak third-quarter results and said it was looking to sell some restaurants and transfer franchised outlets to high-performing operators.

Its U.S. same-store sales fell 5.7 per cent.

Its adjusted revenue fell about 1.9 per cent to US$435.6-million.

The company also said it had signed a letter of intent with Meritage Hospitality Group to acquire up to 163 Wendy’s restaurants.

Trian’s offer came about three months after Wendy’s withdrew its annual forecast, cut its dividend and launched a turnaround plan under new CEO Bob Wright after reporting second-quarter revenue below Wall Street estimates and a decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales.

“Our traffic, our value proposition and franchisee economics are not meeting our expectations,” Wright said in August.

The turnaround was aimed at improving menu value and marketing.

Wendy’s, similar to peers, has rolled out value meals starting at US$4, alongside movie collaborations such as “Minions and Monsters,” to drive traffic and appeal to budget-conscious customers.

As of Dec. 28, 2025, the company had more than 7,000 restaurants worldwide.
